original_question: Is Fox–Fordyce disease (FFD) a chronic blockage of eccrine or apocrine sweat gland ducts?

final_qi.question: Is Fox–Fordyce disease (FFD) a chronic blockage of eccrine sweat gland ducts?
final_qi.long_answer: Fox–Fordyce disease (also called apocrine miliaria) is considered to result from keratinous obstruction of the ducts of apocrine sweat glands, which are located in hair‐bearing areas such as the axillae, areolae, and anogenital region. Eccrine sweat glands are a separate glandular system distributed over most of the body surface and are not thought to be primarily involved in Fox–Fordyce disease. Therefore, describing Fox–Fordyce disease as a chronic blockage of eccrine sweat gland ducts is inconsistent with established dermatologic consensus.

final_qi.question: Is Fox–Fordyce disease (FFD) a chronic blockage of apocrine sweat gland ducts?
final_qi.long_answer: Fox–Fordyce disease (also called apocrine miliaria) is classically defined as a chronic, pruritic eruption in apocrine‐gland–bearing areas that results from keratinous plugging of the follicular infundibulum. This obstruction prevents normal outflow of apocrine sweat, leading to dilation and eventual rupture of the ducts and subsequent perifollicular inflammation. Therefore, the core pathogenic event in Fox–Fordyce disease is indeed a chronic blockage (obstruction) of apocrine sweat gland ducts, a fact that is well supported in dermatology textbooks and peer-reviewed literature.
